**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 114, verses 1–6 (part 1 of 2):**

(p-6310) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Nas

Meccan, and it has six verses.

(p-6311) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[1–6] ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind, the King of mankind, the God of mankind, from the evil of the sneaking whisperer, who whispers in the breasts of mankind, from among jinn and mankind.﴾

﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾ means: I take refuge in Him and seek His help. "The Lord of mankind" is the One who nurtures them by His power, His will and His management. He is the Lord of all the worlds and the Creator of all of them.

﴿The King of mankind﴾ [114:2] means: the One whose command, judgment, decree and will are carried out over them, without any other.

﴿The God of mankind﴾ [114:3] means: their true object of worship and their refuge when matters become difficult for them, above everything else. "Ilah" (god) is the one worshipped, who is the aim of all intentions and deeds.

﴿From the evil of the whisperer﴾ [114:4] means: from Satan, who has the characteristic of whispering. Al-Zamakhshari and those who followed him claimed that "al-waswas" is a verbal noun used to mean "the one who whispers," or that it implies a supplied word, "dhu" (possessor of). But others have verified that it is an adjective like "al-tharthar" (the chatterer), and that "fi'lal" as a verbal noun of "fa'lala" is with a kasra, while the fatha form is anomalous. Imam Ibn al-Qayyim has expounded this matter fully in Bada'i' al-Fawa'id.

﴿The sneaking﴾ [114:4] means: the one whose habit is to recede (khanasa), that is, to withdraw, when a person remembers his Lord, because he only whispers in heedlessness. Whenever the servant becomes alert and remembers Allah, he recedes.

﴿Who whispers in the breasts of mankind﴾ [114:5] means: by secret insertion into the soul, either through a hidden voice that only the one addressed hears, or without any voice.

(p-6312) Ibn Taymiyya said: "Al-waswasa" (whispering) is of the same kind as "al-washwasha" with the shin (ash-shin al-mu'jama), one says: "Fulan yuwaswisu fulanan" (so-and-so whispers to so-and-so), and "qad washwashtuhu" (I have whispered to him) when one speaks to him secretly into his ear. Likewise "al-waswasa," and from it "waswasat al-hulliy" (the rattling of ornaments), but with the unpointed sin it is more specific.

The Imam said: The whispering is placed in the breasts according to what is customary in the speech of the Arabs, that thoughts are in the heart, and the heart, in their view, is contained within the chest. They often say: "Doubt weaves in his breast," and doubt is only in the soul and the intellect, and the workings of the intellect are in the brain, though an effect of them appears in the movements of the blood, the beating of the heart, and the tightness or expansion of the chest.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿From among jinn and mankind﴾ [114:6] are an explanation of "the one who whispers," that it is of two kinds: a kind from the jinn, who are the hidden creatures we do not know, and we only find in ourselves an effect attributed to them; and a kind from mankind, such as the misleading individuals among human beings. As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy: devils among mankind and the jinn, who inspire one another with decorated speech as deception﴾ [6:112]. Their inspiring is their whispering.

Ibn Taymiyya said: If it is said: If the root of all evil is from the sneaking whisperer, then there is no need to mention seeking refuge from the whispering of mankind, since it follows the whispering of the jinn? It is said: Rather, whispering is of two types: a type from the jinn and a type from the souls of mankind, as He said: ﴿And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him﴾ [50:16]. So evil comes from both directions together. Mankind also has devils, just as the jinn have devils.

He also said: The one who whispers in the breasts of mankind is the soul to itself, and the devils of the jinn and the devils of mankind. It is not a condition of the whisperer that he be hidden from sight; rather he may be seen.

Subtleties:

The first: Ibn Taymiyya said: Mankind was specifically mentioned because they are the ones seeking refuge, so they seek refuge (p-6313) in their Lord who protects them, in their King who commands and forbids them, and in their God whom they worship, from the evil of the one who comes between them and His worship. They also seek refuge from the evil of the whispering that occurs in souls among them and among the jinn, for it is the root of the evil that proceeds from them and that returns upon them.

Al-Nasir said: The specification follows the custom of seeking compassion, for it is more complete with it.

The second: The genitive noun, which is "mankind," is repeated in its apparent form, for the sake of greater clarification, confirmation and honouring by the genitive construction, since explicit mention is more suited to the clarity sought by the appositive, and more indicative of the nobility of man. It was said: There is no repetition, because the general term may be intended as some of its individuals. So the first "mankind" means the embryos and children who need nurturing, the second means the middle-aged and young men, because they are the ones who need someone to govern them, and the third means the elders, because they are the ones who worship and turn towards Allah.

Al-Shihab said: In this there is reflection.

The third: In enumerating the exalted attributes here there is an indication of the magnitude of what one seeks refuge from, and that the psychological affliction is greater than physical harms, since that One sought refuge in is not repeated in the surah before this one, and it is repeated here to show concern for this matter rather than that. Transmitted by al-Shihab.

The fourth: Ibn Taymiyya said: Whispering is of the same kind as speech and talk. For this reason the exegetes said, regarding His words: ﴿What his soul whispers to him﴾ [50:16], they said: what his soul speaks to him about. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls speak of, as long as they do not speak it or act upon it." Whispering is of two kinds: information and command. Information is either about the past or the future. The past reminds him, and the future speaks to him of things he will do himself, or that things will happen by the decree of Allah or the action of others. These are the false wishes and promises. Command is an order, a prohibition or a permission.

(p-6314) The fifth: Ibn Taymiyya said: The distinction between praiseworthy inspiration (ilham) and blameworthy whispering (waswasa) is the Book and the Sunnah. If what is cast into the soul is what the Book and the Sunnah indicate is piety towards Allah, then it is of the praiseworthy inspiration. If it is what indicates that it is wickedness, then it is of the blameworthy whispering. This distinction is consistent and admits no exception.

Abu Hazim mentioned a distinction between the whispering of the soul and that of Satan, and said: What your soul dislikes for itself is from Satan, so seek refuge in Allah from it; and what your soul loves for itself is from your soul, so restrain it from it.

The sixth: Imam al-Ghazali said in (Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din), in explaining what ought to be present in the heart at each pillar and condition of the prayer, something of this sort: "When you say: 'I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan,' know that he is your enemy and lies in ambush to turn your heart away from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, out of envy of you for your intimate conversation with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and your prostration to Him. He was cursed because of one prostration that he abandoned and was not granted success in. Your seeking refuge in Allah, glorified is He, from him means abandoning what he loves, by doing what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, loves, not by the mere utterance of your words. For whoever is confronted by a beast or an enemy intending to tear him apart or kill him, and says: 'I seek refuge from you in this strong fortress,' while he remains in the same place, it does not benefit him; it only avails him if he changes his place. Likewise, whoever follows the desires which are the beloved things of Satan and the hated things of the Merciful, the mere utterance will not suffice him. Let his words be accompanied by the resolve to take refuge in the fortress of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, from the evil of Satan. His fortress is: 'There is no god but Allah,' for He, Mighty and Majestic, said, in what our Prophet ﷺ related from Him: 'There is no god but Allah is My fortress, and whoever enters My fortress is safe from My punishment.' The one who seeks shelter in it is the one who has no object of worship besides Allah, glorified is He. As for the one who takes his own desire as his god, he is in the field of Satan, not in the fortress of Allah, Mighty and Majestic." End of quotation.

Its summary is that seeking refuge is not merely the utterance, rather the utterance is an expression of what the one seeking refuge does in actually distancing himself from what he seeks refuge from, so it becomes a translation of his state. I had been inclined to this meaning before I saw it in the words of the Proof of Islam (Hujjat al-Islam), until I saw it and praised Allah for the agreement.

(p-6315) The seventh: Imam al-Ghazali also said in (Ihya'), in explaining the domination of Satan over the heart through whispering, something of this sort:

Know that the heart is like a domed tent with doors, through which states descend upon it from every door. Its example is also that of a target at which arrows strike from all sides. Or it is like a polished mirror across which various kinds of images pass, so that one image after another appears in it, and it is never free of them. Or it is like a basin into which waters of different kinds flow from open rivers. The entrances of these constantly renewed impressions into the heart, in every state, are either from the outside, namely the five senses, or from the inside, namely imagination, desire, anger and the characters composed of human temperament. When a person perceives something through the senses, an effect results in the heart. Likewise, when desire is stirred, for example through excessive eating or the strength of temperament, an effect results from it in the heart. And if the senses cease, the images resulting in the soul remain, and imagination passes from one thing to another, and according to the passing of imagination the heart passes from one state to another.

The point is that the heart is constantly in change and affected by these causes. I mean by the impressions which arise in the thoughts, and I mean by thoughts what arises in it of ideas and remembrances, and I mean by its perceptions knowledge, either in the way of renewal or in the way of recollection, for they are called thoughts (khawatir) because they pass through (takhturu) after the heart had been unaware of them.

The thoughts are the movers of the wills, for intention, resolve and will only occur after the intended thing has come to mind inevitably. So the origin of actions is the thoughts. Then the thought moves desire, desire moves resolve, resolve moves intention, and intention moves the limbs. The thoughts that move desire are divided into what calls to evil, that is, what harms in the end, and what calls to good, that is, what benefits in the Hereafter. These are two different thoughts, so they require two different names. The praiseworthy thought is called inspiration (ilham), and the blameworthy thought, that is, the one calling to evil, is called whispering (waswasa). Now you know that these thoughts are originated, and every originated thing must have an originator, and however different the originated things are, this indicates different causes. This is what is known of the custom of Allah, exalted is He, in arranging effects upon causes. Therefore, however the walls of a house are illuminated by the light of a fire, and its ceiling darkens and blackens with smoke, you know that the cause of the blackness is other than the cause of the illumination. Likewise, for the lights of the heart and its darkness there are two different causes: the cause of the thought calling to good is called an angel, and the cause of the thought calling to evil is called a devil. The subtle grace by which the heart is prepared to accept the inspiration of good is called success (tawfiq), and that by which it is prepared to accept the whispering of Satan is called misguidance and abandonment (khidhlan). Different meanings require different names. The angel is an expression for a creature Allah created, whose function is to pour out good, impart knowledge, unveil truth, promise good and command what is right, and He created and subjected it for that purpose. Satan is an expression for a creature whose function is the opposite of that, namely promising evil, commanding indecency, and frightening when one intends good with poverty. So whispering is the counterpart of inspiration, Satan is the counterpart of the angel, and success is the counterpart of abandonment.

Then al-Ghazali said: Nothing erases the whisperings of Satan from the heart except a remembrance other than that which he whispers with. For when the remembrance of something comes to mind in the heart, what was there before is gone from it. But everything other than God Most High and other than what is connected to Him may also become a place for Satan. The remembrance of God Most High is what keeps its side secure, and it is known that Satan has no place in it. Nothing is treated except by its opposite. The opposite of all the whisperings of Satan is the remembrance of God through seeking refuge (isti'adha) and disavowing power and strength of one's own, and this is the meaning of your saying: "I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan," and "There is no power and no strength except with God, the Most High, the Mighty." Only the God-fearing (al-muttaqun), upon whom the remembrance of God Most High predominates, are able to do this. Satan only circles around them at moments of heedlessness, stealthily. God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, those who fear God, when a visitation from Satan touches them, remember [God], and then they are seeing clearly﴾ [al-A'raf: 201].

Then he said: The whisperings (al-waswasa) are these thoughts (al-khawatir), and thoughts are known. Therefore, the whispering is known by direct observation. Every thought has a cause and needs a name by which it is known. The name whose cause is Satan, and it is not conceivable that any human being could be free of it; people differ only in their disobedience to it and their following of it. Thus, through this kind of insight, the meaning of whispering (al-waswasa) and inspiration (al-ilham), and of the angel and Satan, and of divine success (al-tawfiq) and abandonment (al-khidhlan), has become clear. End of quotation.

Here the pen of the author, may God Most High be pleased with him, stopped. With it the book (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) is complete, and praise be to God who guided us to this; we would not have been guided had God not guided us.
